vjimc-2000-cat1-01.title: Branches of the binary tree
vjimc-2000-cat1-01.body:
**Yes.** Let $Y$ be the set of all finite $0$–$1$ strings (including the empty one). $Y$ is countable: it is the union over $k\ge0$ of the finite sets of strings of length $k$.

For every infinite $0$–$1$ sequence $s=(s_1,s_2,\dots)$ let
$$A_s=\{\,(s_1,\dots,s_k):k\ge0\,\}\subseteq Y$$
be the set of its finite prefixes, and let $\mathcal F=\{A_s\}$.

- **Distinct sequences give sets with finite intersection.** If $s\ne t$, let $j$ be the first index with $s_j\ne t_j$. A common element of $A_s$ and $A_t$ is a string that is a prefix of both, so it has length $<j$. Hence $|A_s\cap A_t|\le j$ is finite. (In particular $A_s\ne A_t$.)
- **$\mathcal F$ is uncountable.** The map $s\mapsto A_s$ is injective, and the set of infinite $0$–$1$ sequences is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument).

So such $Y$ and $\mathcal F$ exist. ∎

vjimc-2000-cat1-01.title: Lattice points near rays
vjimc-2000-cat1-01.body:
Take $Y=\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$, which is countable. For each real $\alpha>0$ put
$$A_\alpha=\{(n,\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor):n\in\mathbb N\},$$
the lattice points just below the ray $y=\alpha x$, and $\mathcal F=\{A_\alpha:\alpha>0\}$.

If $0<\alpha<\beta$ and $(n,m)\in A_\alpha\cap A_\beta$, then $\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor=\lfloor\beta n\rfloor$, so $(\beta-\alpha)n<1$, i.e. $n<\frac1{\beta-\alpha}$. Since the first coordinate determines the point, the intersection is finite. The sets $A_\alpha$ are pairwise distinct (each is infinite, and two of them share only finitely many points), so $\mathcal F$ has the cardinality of $(0,\infty)$ and is uncountable.

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

vjimc-2000-cat1-02.title: Product of divisors and prime exponents
vjimc-2000-cat1-02.body:
**$f(n)\in\mathbb N$.** Let $d_1,\dots,d_{\tau(n)}$ be the divisors of $n$. The map $d\mapsto n/d$ permutes them, so
$$\Big(\prod_{i}d_i\Big)^2=\prod_i d_i\cdot\prod_i\frac n{d_i}=n^{\tau(n)},$$
hence $f(n)=n^{\tau(n)/2}=\prod_i d_i$ is a natural number.

**Injectivity.** Suppose $f(m)=f(n)$; squaring, $m^{\tau(m)}=n^{\tau(n)}$. If one of $m,n$ is $1$ then so is the other (the only $k$ with $k^{\tau(k)}=1$ is $k=1$). Otherwise, by unique factorisation, $m$ and $n$ have the same prime divisors $p_1,\dots,p_k$; write $m=\prod p_i^{\beta_i}$, $n=\prod p_i^{\alpha_i}$ with $\alpha_i,\beta_i\ge1$. Comparing exponents of $p_i$:
$$\beta_i\,\tau(m)=\alpha_i\,\tau(n)\qquad(i=1,\dots,k).$$
By symmetry assume $\tau(m)\ge\tau(n)$. Then $\beta_i\le\alpha_i$ for all $i$, so $m\mid n$. Every divisor of $m$ is then a divisor of $n$, so $\tau(m)\le\tau(n)$. Hence $\tau(m)=\tau(n)$, and then $\beta_i=\alpha_i$ for all $i$, i.e. $m=n$.

So $f$ is an injection $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$. ∎

vjimc-2000-cat1-02.title: Monotonicity along divisibility
vjimc-2000-cat1-02.body:
Integrality is as before ($f(n)$ is the product of the divisors of $n$).

Suppose $f(m)=f(n)$ with $m>n$; then $m\ge2$ and $m^{\tau(m)}=n^{\tau(n)}<m^{\tau(n)}$, so $\tau(m)<\tau(n)$ (if $n=1$ the right side is $1<m^{\tau(m)}$, impossible). As before $m,n$ have the same prime divisors and $\beta_i\tau(m)=\alpha_i\tau(n)$ (notation $n=\prod p_i^{\alpha_i}$, $m=\prod p_i^{\beta_i}$). From $\tau(m)<\tau(n)$ we get $\beta_i>\alpha_i$ for every $i$, so $n\mid m$. Then every divisor of $n$ divides $m$, so $\tau(n)\le\tau(m)$. Contradiction. ∎

vjimc-2000-cat1-03.title: Abel summation
vjimc-2000-cat1-03.body:
**Yes.** In fact Cesàro convergence to $b$ alone implies that the logarithmic means converge to $b$ (boundedness is not even needed).

Let $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^Na_n$ ($S_0=0$) and $b_N=S_N/N\to b$. Summation by parts:
$$\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{a_n}n=\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{S_n-S_{n-1}}n=\frac{S_N}N+\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}S_n\Big(\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\Big)=b_N+\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\frac{b_n}{n+1}.$$

Divide by $\log N$. The term $b_N/\log N\to0$ since $(b_N)$ is bounded. For the sum, write $b_n=b+\varepsilon_n$ with $\varepsilon_n\to0$:
$$\frac1{\log N}\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\frac{b_n}{n+1}=b\cdot\frac{H_N-1}{\log N}+\frac1{\log N}\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\frac{\varepsilon_n}{n+1},$$
where $H_N=\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n$ satisfies $H_N/\log N\to1$. For the error term, fix $K$ and split at $K$:
$$\Big|\frac1{\log N}\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\frac{\varepsilon_n}{n+1}\Big|\le\frac1{\log N}\sum_{n=1}^{K}|\varepsilon_n|+\sup_{j>K}|\varepsilon_j|\cdot\frac{H_N}{\log N}.$$
Letting $N\to\infty$ the first part tends to $0$, so $\limsup\le\sup_{j>K}|\varepsilon_j|$, which tends to $0$ as $K\to\infty$.

Hence $\frac1{\log N}\sum_{n\le N}\frac{a_n}n\to b$; since this limit is $c$ by assumption, $b=c$.

**Answer: Yes, $b=c$.** ∎

vjimc-2000-cat1-04.title: Double counting for each distance
vjimc-2000-cat1-04.body:
It suffices to show that for every distance $d$, the number $R_d$ of red-red pairs at distance $d$ equals the number $B_d$ of blue-blue pairs at distance $d$.

The distance between two vertices depends only on how many steps $m\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ apart they are along the polygon (the chord $2\rho\sin\frac{m\pi}{2n}$ is strictly increasing in $m$ for $1\le m\le n$). Fix $m$ and let $\delta=2$ if $m<n$ and $\delta=1$ if $m=n$ (the diameter): every vertex has exactly $\delta$ vertices at distance $d=d_m$.

Let $X_d$ be the number of red-blue pairs at distance $d$. Count pairs (red vertex $v$, vertex $w$ at distance $d$ from $v$): there are $n\delta$ of them, and each red-red pair is counted twice, each red-blue pair once:
$$2R_d+X_d=n\delta .$$
Doing the same with blue vertices (there are also $n$ of them): $2B_d+X_d=n\delta$. Subtracting, $R_d=B_d$.

So every distance occurs equally often among red-red and blue-blue pairs, and the two sorted sequences coincide. ∎

vjimc-2000-cat1-04.title: Cycles of equal chords (official idea)
vjimc-2000-cat1-04.body:
Fix a step $m\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and let $g=\gcd(2n,m)$. Joining each vertex to the vertex $m$ steps further splits the vertices into $g$ disjoint cycles of length $\frac{2n}g$, whose edges are exactly the chords of length $d_m$ (for $m=n$ each "cycle" is a diameter traversed twice; count each diameter once and the argument below works with halves).

For $m<n$: on the $i$-th cycle let there be $r_i$ red and $b_i$ blue vertices, and let $c_i$ be the number of red→blue changes when going around the cycle (equal to the number of blue→red changes). Each red vertex is followed by a red or a blue vertex, so the number of red-red edges is $r_i-c_i$; similarly there are $b_i-c_i$ blue-blue edges. Summing over the cycles: red-red chords of length $d_m$ number $\sum(r_i-c_i)=n-\sum c_i$, and blue-blue chords $\sum(b_i-c_i)=n-\sum c_i$ — the same.

For $m=n$, the $n$ diameters are red-red, blue-blue or mixed; since there are $n$ red and $n$ blue endpoints, $2R+X=n=2B+X$, so $R=B$. ∎
